chapters.title: Hola and Buenos Días
chapters.label: ch:first-words
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in Spanish, say how I am, and wish them a good day.

payoff.summary: A short doorway greeting: hola, an answer to how you are, and buenos días on the way in.

chapters.title: The Rest of the Greetings
chapters.label: ch:greetings
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone correctly at any hour — morning, afternoon or night — and say why the greeting changes shape.

payoff.summary: The same greeting exchange run three times across the day, choosing the right form for each hour.

chapters.title: Un and Una --- the Other Article
chapters.label: ch:spanish-indefinite-article
chapters.canDo: I can say a day, an afternoon and a night, choosing the article by the noun's gender.

payoff.summary: un is the number one, and English a is the same word worn down.

chapters.title: Saying Your Name
chapters.label: ch:your-name
chapters.canDo: I can say my own name in Spanish.

payoff.summary: Saying Your Name — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: The Three Words for You
chapters.label: ch:three-yous
chapters.canDo: I can choose between tú and usted, and recognise vos.

payoff.summary: The Three Words for You — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: Asking Someone's Name
chapters.label: ch:asking-a-name
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone's name in either register and say it was a pleasure.

payoff.summary: Asking Someone's Name — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: Thank You, Yes, and No
chapters.label: ch:thank-you
chapters.canDo: I can thank someone, answer when I am thanked, and say yes or no.

payoff.summary: Thanks, the answer to thanks, and the two words that let you accept or decline.

chapters.title: How Are You
chapters.label: ch:how-are-you
chapters.canDo: I can ask a stranger how they are.

payoff.summary: Greeting plus the question that opens almost every conversation.

chapters.title: Answering, and Handing It Back
chapters.label: ch:answering
chapters.canDo: I can answer how I am, choose my register, and return the question.

payoff.summary: The answer, the register choice inside it, and handing the question back.

chapters.title: The Written Accent
chapters.label: ch:written-accent
chapters.canDo: I can hear where a Spanish word is stressed and see why the accent is written.

payoff.summary: The Written Accent — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: Enye and the Upside-Down Marks
chapters.label: ch:enye-and-marks
chapters.canDo: I can read and write ñ and the upside-down question and exclamation marks.

payoff.summary: Enye and the Upside-Down Marks — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: Goodbye
chapters.label: ch:goodbye
chapters.canDo: I can end a conversation, and I know the word every softer goodbye is built from.

payoff.summary: Goodbye — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: Until When
chapters.label: ch:until-when
chapters.canDo: I can pick the farewell that matches when I will next see someone.

payoff.summary: Until When — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: A Coffee, Please
chapters.label: ch:a-coffee
chapters.canDo: I can ask for something politely.

payoff.summary: A Coffee, Please — the chapter run end to end.

chapters.title: When You Don't Understand
chapters.label: ch:repair
chapters.canDo: I can say that I did not understand, and ask for it more slowly.

payoff.summary: The two sentences that rescue a conversation, and the thanks that closes it.

chapters.title: Your First Verb, and the Form That Means I
chapters.label: ch:first-verb
chapters.canDo: I can say what I do, in one word, with no pronoun at all.

payoff.summary: One word, one whole sentence — and why English cannot do the same.

chapters.title: Talking to a Friend
chapters.label: ch:hablas
chapters.canDo: I can say what a friend does, using the tu form of an -ar verb.

payoff.summary: The -as ending, and the one English ending that survives beside it.

chapters.title: He, She, and the Polite You
chapters.label: ch:habla
chapters.canDo: I can say what someone else does, and address someone respectfully, with one form.

payoff.summary: One form doing three jobs, and the vuestra merced fossil behind it.

chapters.title: Review --- The Three Forms Side by Side
chapters.label: ch:review-ar-singular
chapters.canDo: I can hold all three singular -ar forms at once and choose between them without stopping.

payoff.summary: The first paradigm table in the book, arriving only after all three of its cells are owned.

chapters.title: Trabajar --- Work, and the Torture Device Behind It
chapters.label: ch:spanish-trabajar
chapters.canDo: I can say what I do for work with a second regular -ar verb.

payoff.summary: tripalium, a three-stake device, is why work and travail are the same word.

chapters.title: Estudiar --- Studying Is Being Eager
chapters.label: ch:spanish-estudiar
chapters.canDo: I can say what I study, with a third regular -ar verb and no new pattern.

payoff.summary: studere, to be eager - the root under student, studio and studious.

chapters.title: Espanol, and Your First Built Sentence
chapters.label: ch:spanish-espanol
chapters.canDo: I can name the language and build a whole sentence from parts I chose myself.

payoff.summary: Hispania to espanol, and the first sentence assembled rather than memorised.

chapters.title: -cion --- About Two Thousand Words, At Once
chapters.label: ch:friend-cion
chapters.canDo: I can turn an English -tion word into Spanish and know its gender without being told.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C56-cion: convert an English -tion word, give the gender, and say why the correspondence is a rule.
payoff.note: The highest-reach lesson in the book so far: one ending, roughly two thousand words, and a gender that never has to be decided. Not a resemblance -- Latin -tionem, inherited by Spanish and borrowed by English.

chapters.title: -dad --- Twelve Hundred More
chapters.label: ch:friend-dad
chapters.canDo: I can read a -dad word I have never met, and say why it looks less like its English partner.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C56-dad: convert university, read realidad unseen, and explain the uneven erosion.
payoff.note: Harder to spot than -cion because English wore -tatem down further, through French, to -ty. Same relationship, more erosion on one side.

chapters.title: -mente --- With No Upper Limit
chapters.label: ch:friend-mente
chapters.canDo: I can build an adverb from any adjective, and say why the adjective goes feminine first.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C56-mente: build rapidamente, explain the feminine step, and say what the word literally means.
payoff.note: A machine rather than a decoder: its reach is however many adjectives the reader ends up holding. The feminine step is not arbitrary -- mente was a feminine NOUN, and the agreement outlived it.

chapters.title: Review --- Three Endings
chapters.label: ch:review-friends
chapters.canDo: I can name the three endings, their partners, and which give gender for free.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C56-repaso-amigos: give the three pairs and distinguish a decoder from a machine.
payoff.note: States the arithmetic plainly: three chapters reach further than every vocabulary lesson in the book combined, which changes what a reader should expect the rest of it to be.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Reading What You Were Never Taught
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-friends
chapters.canDo: I can read a sentence containing words no lesson has taught me.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C56-sintesis-leer: read a four-new-word sentence and say what let you read it.
payoff.note: First chapter that asks the reader to read words nobody taught them. Also warns, at no cost, that the endings are reliable rather than perfect, so the false friends later land as memorable rather than as a betrayal.

chapters.title: F to H --- Why the H Says Nothing
chapters.label: ch:sound-f-h
chapters.canDo: I can decode an unfamiliar h- word by putting an f back, and say why the h is silent.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C57-f-a-h: say why the h is silent, name hablar's English friend, and decode hierro unseen.
payoff.note: Pays off a bare fact held since chapter one. The silent h is a gravestone: Latin f- weakened to a breath and then to nothing, and the spelling outlived the sound. Also states its own limits -- hola and hasta are not dead f-words.

chapters.title: Cl-, Pl-, Fl- to Ll-
chapters.label: ch:sound-cluster-ll
chapters.canDo: I can try three Latin clusters on an unfamiliar ll- word and find the English cousin.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C57-ll: name llamar's cousins, give the three clusters, and decode llave.
payoff.note: Three starting points, one destination -- untidy, and useful because of it: an unfamiliar ll- word gives the reader three English shapes to try. Also names what all three sound laws share: Spanish inherited and eroded, English borrowed later and stayed nearer the Latin.

chapters.title: Es- --- the Vowel Spanish Put in Front
chapters.label: ch:es-inicial
chapters.canDo: I can strip the e- from a Spanish word beginning es- plus a consonant and recognise the English word underneath.

payoff.summary: Decode estacion, estudiante and espacio by taking the e- off the front.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- The Decoder
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-sound-laws
chapters.canDo: I can decode unfamiliar Spanish with three sound laws and three endings.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C57-sintesis-descifrar: decode hoja and lleno, read a two-ending phrase, and say what a word that resists every rule suggests.
payoff.note: Six rules together. Deliberately exact about what a decoder is NOT -- a reading tool, mostly first guesses -- because overclaiming it disappoints at the worst moment. What actually changes is that an unfamiliar word stops being a wall.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- The Same Conversation, Twice
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-ar-singular
chapters.canDo: I can hold one short conversation both warmly and respectfully, changing only the verb ending.

payoff.summary: The register choice carried entirely by one letter - and now with something real to say.

chapters.title: Putting the -ar Verbs to Work
chapters.label: ch:spanish-ar-practice
chapters.canDo: I can use several -ar verbs in real sentences.

payoff.summary: The -ar present tense in action across the verbs of the last chapters.

chapters.title: Comer --- the Second Verb Family, One Slot at a Time
chapters.label: ch:spanish-comer
chapters.canDo: I can use all three singular forms of a regular -er verb, having built each one separately.

payoff.summary: The -er singular, earned a slot at a time - and the yo ending that never changed.

chapters.title: Vivir --- the Family That Costs Nothing
chapters.label: ch:spanish-vivir
chapters.canDo: I can use the singular of a regular -ir verb, and say why it asked me to learn no new form.

payoff.summary: In the singular the -ir endings ARE the -er endings; the families part company only in the plural.

chapters.title: Beber, and Two Ways to Ask
chapters.label: ch:spanish-beber-preguntas
chapters.canDo: I can say what I drink, and ask what and where with que and donde.

payoff.summary: A second -er verb that needs no new pattern, and the two question words that turn the forms outward.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Asking, and Answering
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-three-families
chapters.canDo: I can hold a short exchange about what someone drinks and where they live, using all three verb families.

payoff.summary: Three families and two question words, and every word in the dialogue self-built.

chapters.title: Hablamos --- the First Form That Is Not About One Person
chapters.label: ch:spanish-hablamos
chapters.canDo: I can say what we do, with the -amos ending.

payoff.summary: -mos is Latin's -mus, barely changed in two thousand years.

chapters.title: Hablan --- They, and Ustedes
chapters.label: ch:spanish-hablan
chapters.canDo: I can say what they do, and address any group as ustedes.

payoff.summary: ustedes is vuestras mercedes - so it takes the they form for the same reason usted takes the he form.

chapters.title: Hablais --- the Form Spain Keeps
chapters.label: ch:spanish-hablais
chapters.canDo: I can recognise the vosotros form and say where it is used.

payoff.summary: vos + otros, added in Spain to keep the plural apart from a singular vos the Americas kept instead.

chapters.title: Review --- the Whole Present Tense
chapters.label: ch:spanish-review-present-complete
chapters.canDo: I can produce all six present-tense forms of a regular -ar verb.

payoff.summary: The first complete paradigm in the book - withheld for thirty-two chapters until every box in it was earned.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- the Same Sentence, Two Continents
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-plural-you
chapters.canDo: I can choose between vosotros and ustedes by where I am, and say that neither corrects the other.

payoff.summary: The first choice in this book decided by geography rather than meaning.

chapters.title: Where -er and -ir Part Company
chapters.label: ch:spanish-er-ir-1pl
chapters.canDo: I can say what we eat and what we live, and explain why the singular hid the difference.

payoff.summary: comemos and vivimos: one vowel apart, audible only because the ending is stressed.

chapters.title: Comeis and Vivis
chapters.label: ch:spanish-er-ir-2pl
chapters.canDo: I can recognise both vosotros forms and say that they are the second and last difference.

payoff.summary: Latin's -tis, collapsed two ways: -eis for one family, -is for the other.

chapters.title: Comen and Viven --- Agreeing Again
chapters.label: ch:spanish-er-ir-3pl
chapters.canDo: I can say what they eat and what they live, with one ending shared by both families.

payoff.summary: After two chapters apart the families fall back into step and stay there.

chapters.title: Review --- the Present Tense, Whole
chapters.label: ch:spanish-review-present-all
chapters.canDo: I can conjugate any regular Spanish verb in the present, in any of the three families.

payoff.summary: Eighteen forms, every one built separately before it appeared in the grid.

chapters.title: Numbers, and How Old You Are
chapters.label: ch:numbers-and-age
chapters.canDo: I can count from one through ten and use singular forms of tener to ask and answer age with a number I know.

payoff.summary: Count from one through ten, move among tengo, tienes, and tiene, then ask and answer age with the number frame taught in the chapter.

chapters.title: Ser and Estar --- Two Ways to Be
chapters.label: ch:ser-y-estar
chapters.canDo: I can identify someone, state origin, check wellbeing, and give a location by choosing a learned singular form of ser or estar.

payoff.summary: Identify Ana, state an origin with soy de, check a current state, and locate Ana with está en using only previously introduced vocabulary and singular forms.

chapters.title: Going, and the Future You Can Already Say
chapters.label: ch:ir-y-futuro
chapters.canDo: I can ask where someone is going, say what a singular person is going to do, and mark a known singular noun with mi, tu, or su.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C10-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with singular ir, ir a plus a known infinitive, and mi, tu, or su before café.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all nine Chapter-10 atoms and deliberately stays on the singular-person, known-infinitive, and known-noun frontier.

chapters.title: Ser in the Plural
chapters.label: ch:spanish-ser-plural
chapters.canDo: I can use all six present forms of ser, and say why no two of them look alike.

payoff.summary: Two Latin verbs in one paradigm - and the seam between them is visible at eres.

chapters.title: Profesor --- and the Article Spanish Leaves Out
chapters.label: ch:profesor
chapters.canDo: I can say what someone does for a living with ser and no article.

payoff.summary: I can say what someone does for a living with ser and no article.

chapters.title: Estudiante --- a Word You Can Build
chapters.label: ch:estudiante
chapters.canDo: I can build a person-word from a verb with -ante, and read it as English -ant.

payoff.summary: I can build a person-word from a verb with -ante, and read it as English -ant.

chapters.title: -ista --- Jobs You Can Already Read
chapters.label: ch:ista
chapters.canDo: I can read an -ista word as English -ist without being taught it.

payoff.summary: I can read an -ista word as English -ist without being taught it.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Saying What People Do
chapters.label: ch:sintesis-trabajo
chapters.canDo: I can say what I and others do, and turn the question back.

payoff.summary: I can say what I and others do, and turn the question back.

chapters.title: Estar in the Plural
chapters.label: ch:spanish-estar-plural
chapters.canDo: I can use all six present forms of estar, and say why its plural is regular where ser's is not.

payoff.summary: One Latin verb against two - which is the whole reason one paradigm is plain and the other is not.

chapters.title: La Casa --- Your First Everyday Noun
chapters.label: ch:noun-casa
chapters.canDo: I can say la casa and tengo una casa, using the article and gender rules I already hold.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C43-casa: produce la casa and tengo una casa, and say what casa meant in Latin.
payoff.note: The chapter adds a noun and no grammar: the article, gender and tener machinery were all in place, and had nothing ordinary to act on.

chapters.title: El Libro --- And a Word Made of Tree Bark
chapters.label: ch:noun-libro
chapters.canDo: I can say el libro and tengo un libro, and contrast it with la casa as a gender pair.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C43-libro: produce el libro and tengo un libro, and say what Latin liber originally named.
payoff.note: Pairing one masculine and one feminine everyday noun is the point: from here every gender-dependent rule has two plain test cases.

chapters.title: Grande --- the First Word for What a Thing Is Like
chapters.label: ch:grande
chapters.canDo: I can describe a thing with an adjective after the noun.

payoff.summary: I can describe a thing with an adjective after the noun.

chapters.title: Cansado --- a State, Not a Quality
chapters.label: ch:cansado
chapters.canDo: I can say how I am right now with estar and an adjective.

payoff.summary: I can say how I am right now with estar and an adjective.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Describing Things
chapters.label: ch:sintesis-describir
chapters.canDo: I can choose ser or estar with an adjective and make it agree.

payoff.summary: I can choose ser or estar with an adjective and make it agree.

chapters.title: -oso --- a Shelf of Words You Were Never Taught
chapters.label: ch:oso
chapters.canDo: I can read an -oso word as English -ous, make it agree, and choose ser or estar for it.

payoff.summary: Read misterioso, make comida deliciosa agree, and pick estar for nervioso.

chapters.title: -ncia --- Turning a Quality into a Thing
chapters.label: ch:ncia
chapters.canDo: I can read an -ncia word as English -nce, know it is feminine, and describe it.

payoff.summary: Read preferencia, choose la for distancia, and say una diferencia grande.

chapters.title: -ario --- the Eighth and Last Ending
chapters.label: ch:ario
chapters.canDo: I can read an -ario word as English -ary and tell noun from adjective.

payoff.summary: I can read an -ario word as English -ary and tell noun from adjective.

chapters.title: Review --- the Eight Endings
chapters.label: ch:repaso-ocho
chapters.canDo: I can sort the eight endings by what they make and know which decide gender.

payoff.summary: I can sort the eight endings by what they make and know which decide gender.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Reading a Paragraph
chapters.label: ch:sintesis-ocho
chapters.canDo: I can read a paragraph of Spanish I was never taught.

payoff.summary: I can read a paragraph of Spanish I was never taught.

chapters.title: Falsos Amigos --- the Words That Obey and Lie
chapters.label: ch:falsos-amigos
chapters.canDo: I can spot a false friend by checking a decoded word against the sentence.

payoff.summary: Recognise exito, actualmente and libreria as words that obey the rules and mean something else.

chapters.title: Tener in the Plural, and the Stem-Change Rule
chapters.label: ch:spanish-tener-plural
chapters.canDo: I can use tener in every person, and state when a stem changes and when it does not.

payoff.summary: The stem breaks exactly where it is stressed - so nosotros and vosotros never break, in any verb.

chapters.title: Ir in the Plural --- a Verb That Is Not Ir
chapters.label: ch:spanish-ir-plural
chapters.canDo: I can use ir in every person, and say why its present belongs to a different verb.

payoff.summary: The present of ir is regular for vadere - and the four commonest verbs are now complete.

chapters.title: Verbs That Break in the Middle --- the Stem Changers
chapters.label: ch:stem-changes
chapters.canDo: I can express singular wanting and ability, compare the learned e-to-ie and o-to-ue changes, and say our with a known singular noun.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C11-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate singular querer and poder, the learned vowel-change contrast, and nuestro or nuestra before a known singular noun.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all eleven Chapter-11 atoms and deliberately leaves plural persons, plural possessive agreement, and untaught nouns for later lessons.

chapters.title: Hacer, Decir, and the -go Verb Club
chapters.label: ch:yo-go-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can use the three learned singular forms of hacer and decir and compare tengo, hago, and digo without predicting unseen verbs.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C12-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with known words and only the learned singular person frame.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all eight Chapter-12 atoms and deliberately leaves plural persons, weather and homework vocabulary, and unseen yo-go verbs for later lessons.

chapters.title: Poner --- Putting, and the Root Under Position
chapters.label: ch:spanish-poner
chapters.canDo: I can say what I put, with the -go yo form and regular forms elsewhere.

payoff.summary: pongo in the yo slot, pones and pone everywhere else.

chapters.title: Salir --- Leaving
chapters.label: ch:spanish-salir
chapters.canDo: I can say that I leave, and use the regular forms for anyone else.

payoff.summary: salgo in the yo slot; sales and sale behave normally.

chapters.title: Venir --- Coming
chapters.label: ch:spanish-venir
chapters.canDo: I can say that I come, and hear the stem break in the other two forms.

payoff.summary: vengo, then vienes and viene with the ie break.

chapters.title: Review --- Six Verbs, One Ending
chapters.label: ch:spanish-review-yo-go
chapters.canDo: I can name all six -go verbs and say why the list is closed.

payoff.summary: The club is complete at six - and it was never a club, only six unrelated verbs that converged.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- You, and Somebody Else
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-yo-go
chapters.canDo: I can say the same thing about myself and about someone else, and know which of the two is irregular.

payoff.summary: The oddity lives only in the yo slot - the form a beginner says most.

chapters.title: Deriving the Rest
chapters.label: ch:spanish-derive-plurals
chapters.canDo: I can produce the plural of any irregular verb in this book from rules, and conjugate a verb I was never shown.

payoff.summary: Three rules generate the whole present tense - and a system, unlike a table, works on words it has never seen.

chapters.title: La Comida --- A Noun You Can Build
chapters.label: ch:noun-comida
chapters.canDo: I can build comida from comer with -ida, and know that nouns made this way are feminine.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C43-comida: derive comida from comer and say what gender the -ida ending guarantees.
payoff.note: The ending matters more than the word: it is the first noun the reader could have produced without being told, and it carries its gender with it.

chapters.title: Las --- The Plural Article That Behaves
chapters.label: ch:articles-las
chapters.canDo: I can say las casas and las comidas, putting the plural -s on both the article and the noun.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C44-las: produce las casas and las comidas and say how many new rules the chapter added.
payoff.note: Adds no rule. The chapter-one -s rule turns out to apply to the article as well, which is agreement doing what it has always done.

chapters.title: Los --- The One That Does Not Add -s
chapters.label: ch:articles-los
chapters.canDo: I can say los libros and explain why the masculine plural article is not els.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C44-los: produce los libros, give all four articles, and say why el does not simply take an -s.
payoff.note: The only article that changes more than its ending. Explained as the third appearance of one sound change: the masculine forms lost a vowel the feminine ones never had to lose.

chapters.title: -es --- The Plural Chapter One Promised
chapters.label: ch:plural-es
chapters.canDo: I can form the plural of a word ending in a consonant, and say why the extra vowel is there.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C44-plural-es: pluralise espanol, name the word that has carried this rule since long before the chapter, and say why -s alone will not do.
payoff.note: Delivers a rule chapter one explicitly deferred. Anchored on ustedes, which the reader has used for fifty chapters without being told it was the consonant plural.

chapters.title: Review --- All Four Words for The
chapters.label: ch:review-articles
chapters.canDo: I can give el, la, los and las and state the plural rule including its consonant repair.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C44-repaso-articulos: give the four articles in order and state the plural rule in one sentence.
payoff.note: First chapter in which all four definite articles may appear together: the last of them was earned two chapters earlier.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- More Than One
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-more-than-one
chapters.canDo: I can contrast a bare plural with a definite plural, and know that the indefinite article is dropped rather than pluralised.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C44-sintesis-mas-de-uno: say tengo libros and tengo los libros and explain what separates them.
payoff.note: The communicative payoff of the plural arc: one article pluralises and the other leaves, and the difference is definiteness, which English marks without ever explaining.

chapters.title: Lo --- Saying It Without Naming It
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-lo
chapters.canDo: I can replace a masculine noun already named with lo, in front of the verb.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C42-lo: turn Tengo el libro into Lo tengo, and name the article that shares lo's Latin ancestor.
payoff.note: The pre-verb slot is not new: it has been held since me llamo. Only the word filling it is.

chapters.title: La --- The Pronoun Carries What Left
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-la
chapters.canDo: I can replace a feminine noun with la, and explain that the pronoun carries a gender the sentence no longer states.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C42-la: turn Hago la comida into La hago and say what decides between lo and la.
payoff.note: First point in the path where a word must remember a property of something that has been removed from the sentence.

chapters.title: Me and Te --- The Two People Talking
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-me-te
chapters.canDo: I can say te quiero and me quieres, and tell the doer form apart from the object form.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C42-te: produce te quiero and me quieres, and name the English pair that matches tu and te.
payoff.note: Exactly one new form. Me contributes a second use of a word held since chapter four, which is why both lessons fit one chapter without crowding it.

chapters.title: Review --- Four Pronouns, One Slot
chapters.label: ch:review-direct-object
chapters.canDo: I can name me, te, lo and la and say which of them a noun decides.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C42-repaso-objeto: give all four pronouns and identify the single question that chooses between them.
payoff.note: Nothing is introduced. The table is a recap of four cells built one per chapter, which is why it is allowed to appear at all.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Saying It Once
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-say-it-once
chapters.canDo: I can answer a yes/no question about a thing already named without naming it again.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C42-sintesis-decirlo-una-vez: answer Tienes el libro and Haces la comida with lo tengo and la hago, and say what was wrong with the grammatically correct version.
payoff.note: No new forms. The subject is the communicative function no table can drill: noticing that a thing has already been named.

chapters.title: Nos --- Us, and the Word Inside -mos
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-nos
chapters.canDo: I can say nos quieren, and say what nosotros is made of.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C45-nos: produce nos quieren and name the verb ending that is the same ancient word.
payoff.note: Also closes a gap: the reader has used the -mos ending for thirty chapters and had never met the word nosotros.

chapters.title: Los and Las --- Them, Derived
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-plural
chapters.canDo: I can make any direct object pronoun plural, and say why the pronoun is tidier than the article.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C45-los-las: produce los tengo and las hago, and explain why lo needed no repair in the plural when el did.
payoff.note: The reader produces both forms in the warm-up before being given them. The etymology pays off a puzzle set two arcs earlier.

chapters.title: Os --- You All, in Spain
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-os
chapters.canDo: I can use os for a group in Spain and los or las everywhere else.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C45-os: say os quiero and its non-peninsular equivalent, and name the older word os is worn down from.
payoff.note: Second time the course splits on geography rather than meaning, and the same word vos accounts for os, vosotros and Argentine vos.

chapters.title: Review --- All Eight
chapters.label: ch:review-object-complete
chapters.canDo: I can give all eight direct object pronouns and say which four depend on a noun.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C45-repaso-ocho: give the eight pronouns and identify the four that a noun decides.
payoff.note: Nine chapters of one cell at a time; this is the first page on which all eight appear together, and two of them were never taught at all.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- The Conversation Without Them
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-without-repeating
chapters.canDo: I can carry a four-turn exchange using pronouns, and say what a pronoun promises the listener.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C45-sintesis-sin-repetir: run the exchange with pronouns and say what goes wrong when the gender points at nothing.
payoff.note: States the cost as well as the benefit: a pronoun buys speed and is paid for in attention, which is the skill no grid can carry.

chapters.title: Le --- To Him, To Her, To You
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-le
chapters.canDo: I can say le digo, and know that le does not mark gender.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C46-le: produce le digo, say how many genders le has, and name the Latin case it comes from.
payoff.note: After four chapters of choosing between lo and la by gender, le asks for nothing: one form covers him, her and usted. Latin's dative illi survives here whole.

chapters.title: Les --- And What the Second System Costs
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-les
chapters.canDo: I can say les digo and name the four pronouns that are identical in both object systems.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C46-les: produce les digo and say how many genuinely new words the indirect set adds.
payoff.note: The arithmetic is the lesson: a second complete table costs exactly two new words, because me, te, nos and os do both jobs unchanged.

chapters.title: Which One Is the Verb Asking For?
chapters.label: ch:which-object
chapters.canDo: I can decide between the direct and indirect pronoun by asking one question of the verb.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C46-cual-pide: state the test, apply it to hablar and tener, and say why le veo is not an error in Madrid.
payoff.note: Replaces a verb-by-verb list with a test the reader can run, and names leismo honestly rather than letting it arrive later as a contradiction.

chapters.title: Review --- Two Systems, Two New Words
chapters.label: ch:review-both-objects
chapters.canDo: I can give both object pronoun sets and say which row is the only one where they differ in shape.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C46-repaso-dos-sistemas: give the six indirect pronouns and count the distinct shapes across both tables.
payoff.note: Twelve cells carried by nine shapes. The only asymmetry is the him/her row, where the direct set marks gender and the indirect set does not.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- The Thing and the Person
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-two-sets
chapters.canDo: I can use both sets in one exchange and say what decides between them.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C46-sintesis-dar-y-decir: run the four-turn exchange and say what separates lo from le.
payoff.note: First choice in the book that nothing on the page can settle: same slot, same length, same Latin ancestor, and only meaning tells them apart.

chapters.title: Me Lo --- Both at Once
chapters.label: ch:double-object-order
chapters.canDo: I can put two object pronouns in front of one verb, in the right order.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C47-me-lo: produce te lo digo and me la haces, and say which pronoun leads.
payoff.note: No new pronoun. The fixed order is smaller to learn than English's free one, and the lesson says so.

chapters.title: Se Lo --- The Pair That Does Not Exist
chapters.label: ch:se-for-le
chapters.canDo: I can turn le or les into se in front of lo, la, los or las.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C47-se-lo: produce se lo digo, name the four words that trigger the change, and count the readings se lo digo allows.
payoff.note: The reader is asked to say le lo digo aloud first; the mouth objects before the grammar does.

chapters.title: Why Se? --- Gelo, and a Collision
chapters.label: ch:etymon-gelo
chapters.canDo: I can say why le becomes se, and that this se is not the reflexive one.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C47-por-que-se: name the Old Spanish form, and say whether the se of se lo digo is the se of se llama.
payoff.note: Removes a confusion most learners carry for years: two unrelated words, Latin se and Latin illi, collided by sound in the sixteenth century.

chapters.title: Review --- The Pairs
chapters.label: ch:review-double-object
chapters.canDo: I can generate every permitted pair of object pronouns from two facts.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C47-repaso-dobles: state the two facts that generate the table and say how many new pronouns the arc added.
payoff.note: Answer: none. One order and one substitution, and the substitution is an accident of medieval pronunciation rather than a rule.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Two at a Time
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-double-object
chapters.canDo: I can carry a four-turn exchange in which almost no noun appears.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C47-sintesis-dos-a-la-vez: produce se la hago and say how many words in it name anything.
payoff.note: Three words carrying a person and a thing, neither named. The cost is doubled too: two pronouns are two promises that both things are still in the room.

chapters.title: The Preterite --- Your First Past Tense
chapters.label: ch:preterite
chapters.canDo: I can use the singular completed past of ser or ir and the known regular -ar verb hablar.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C14-practice and distinguish fui/fuiste/fue from hablé/hablaste/habló using known words, context, and written stress.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all six Chapter-14 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers plural persons, other past-tense verb classes, and new time, place, or person vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Regular Preterite
chapters.label: ch:spanish-preterito-regular
chapters.canDo: I can say what I did with a regular -er or -ir verb, and place the written accent correctly.

payoff.summary: -er and -ir agree again, and the accent marks the stressed final vowel.

chapters.title: The Strong Preterites
chapters.label: ch:spanish-preterito-fuerte
chapters.canDo: I can use tuve, hice and estuve, and hear that their stress sits on the stem.

payoff.summary: Latin's own perfect, carried through on verbs too heavily used to be rebuilt.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- You Can Hear Which Past It Is
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-preterito
chapters.canDo: I can tell a regular preterite from a strong one by ear, and say why only one of them carries an accent.

payoff.summary: The accent is the stress written down: ending-stressed regular, stem-stressed strong.

chapters.title: The Imperfect --- What Used to Happen
chapters.label: ch:spanish-imperfecto
chapters.canDo: I can describe an ongoing or habitual past with a regular verb from any family.

payoff.summary: -aba and -ia, and -er and -ir agreeing once again.

chapters.title: Ver --- Seeing
chapters.label: ch:spanish-ver
chapters.canDo: I can say what I see, with a verb whose stem keeps a letter Latin had.

payoff.summary: videre, and the e that other verbs dropped but ver kept.

chapters.title: The Only Three Irregulars
chapters.label: ch:spanish-imperfecto-irregulares
chapters.canDo: I can use era, iba and veia, and know that no fourth irregular imperfect exists.

payoff.summary: erat and ibat worn straight through from Latin, never tidied up.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Three Exceptions, and No Others
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-imperfecto
chapters.canDo: I can use the imperfect freely, knowing its complete irregular inventory is three verbs.

payoff.summary: The exceptions are the words you use most - which is the reason they are exceptions.

chapters.title: Hablaba and Hablo --- Two Ways of Looking
chapters.label: ch:aspect-not-time
chapters.canDo: I can say that the two past tenses differ in viewpoint rather than in time.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C48-dos-miradas: say whether the two pasts differ in when, and identify which one views an event from outside.
payoff.note: No new form. The chapter's work is to stop the reader looking for a rule about time, because there is not one.

chapters.title: Cuando --- Both Pasts in One Sentence
chapters.label: ch:cuando
chapters.canDo: I can join a scene and an event with cuando, using the right tense for each.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C48-cuando: build estudiaba cuando hablo Ana and say which tense sets the room.
payoff.note: Fills a gap while it is needed: cuando was never taught, and the contrast cannot be shown in a single sentence without it.

chapters.title: Tenia and Tuve --- When the Tense Changes the Meaning
chapters.label: ch:aspect-changes-meaning
chapters.canDo: I can say why tuve una casa means I got one, and predict what a state verb's preterite will mean.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C48-tenia-tuve: contrast tenia and tuve, and say what any state verb's preterite will mean.
payoff.note: Derives the meaning change from the aspect rule rather than listing it: a state forced to have edges gives you the moment it began.

chapters.title: Review --- One Question, Three Answers
chapters.label: ch:review-two-pasts
chapters.canDo: I can state the single question that chooses between the two past tenses.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C48-repaso-dos-pasados: state the question, identify the scene verb, and name the pair that changes meaning.
payoff.note: Deliberately gives a question rather than a list of trigger words, because trigger lists fail exactly where the choice is interesting.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- A Small Story
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-story
chapters.canDo: I can narrate four sentences using both past tenses, with a background and a foreground.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C48-sintesis-una-historia: identify the two layers of the story and say why tuve belongs to the foreground.
payoff.note: First narration in the book. The same verb appears in both layers doing different jobs, and nothing about it is irregular.

chapters.title: Hablado, Comido, Vivido --- The Participle
chapters.label: ch:participle
chapters.canDo: I can form the participle of any regular verb, and know it never changes for person.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-participio: form the three participles and say whether the form changes with the speaker.
payoff.note: One new ending and one the reader can predict: -er and -ir merge here for the same reason they merged in the preterite.

chapters.title: He Hablado --- A Verb With No Meaning Left
chapters.label: ch:perfect-first-person
chapters.canDo: I can say he hablado, and say what haber contributes to it.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-he-hablado: produce he hablado espanol and say what haber means there.
payoff.note: Answers the question learners actually have: haber means nothing here. Spanish gave the meaning to tener, exactly as English hollowed out have.

chapters.title: Has, Ha, Hemos, Habeis, Han
chapters.label: ch:perfect-complete
chapters.canDo: I can use every form of haber with a participle.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-haber-completo: give all six forms and say why haber is shorter than an ordinary verb.
payoff.note: Five of six forms are one syllable, and the reason is frequency -- the same reason ser and ir are worn strange.

chapters.title: Hecho, Dicho, Visto, Puesto
chapters.label: ch:irregular-participles
chapters.canDo: I can use the four irregular participles and say why those four.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-participios-irregulares: give the four forms, name the English noun that is hecho, and say why these four break the rule.
payoff.note: They are not broken forms; they are Latin participles inherited whole, older than the -ado/-ido machinery that replaced them everywhere else.

chapters.title: Review --- A Tense You Build
chapters.label: ch:review-perfect
chapters.canDo: I can name the two pieces of the perfect and say which carries the person.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-repaso-perfecto: name the two pieces and say why this tense cost less than the present or preterite.
payoff.note: Names the shape: a tense that is BUILT costs a fixed amount, not a per-verb amount -- and Spanish reuses these same two pieces for more tenses later.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Two Shores, Two Answers
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-perfect
chapters.canDo: I can say what the perfect does that the preterite does not, and that today takes different tenses in Spain and Latin America.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C49-sintesis-dos-orillas: contrast he comido with comi, and say which tense Madrid and Mexico City choose for today.
payoff.note: Third split decided by geography rather than meaning, after vosotros and os. Stated with a default so the reader is not left choosing in the dark.

chapters.title: The Future --- Saying What Will Happen
chapters.label: ch:spanish-futuro
chapters.canDo: I can say what I will do, in the singular, across all three verb families.

payoff.summary: The future endings ride on the whole infinitive, one family at a time.

chapters.title: The Conditional --- Saying What Would Happen
chapters.label: ch:spanish-condicional
chapters.canDo: I can say what I would do, in the singular, across all three verb families.

payoff.summary: The same infinitive, a different auxiliary tense on the end.

chapters.title: One Stem, Two Tenses
chapters.label: ch:spanish-future-conditional-stems
chapters.canDo: I can use the irregular stems that serve the future and the conditional alike.

payoff.summary: hare, tendre, podre - stems shared by both tenses, so learning one buys the other.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Promising, and Supposing
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-future-conditional
chapters.canDo: I can choose between a promise and a supposition, and say why the endings differ.

payoff.summary: Haber glued on twice - present for the promise, past for the guess.

chapters.title: Wanting, Not Asserting
chapters.label: ch:spanish-quiero-que
chapters.canDo: I can tell an asserted event apart from a wanted one, and say why the verb changes.

payoff.summary: Hablas espanol asserts; quiero que hables asserts nothing at all.

chapters.title: The Subjunctive, Regular
chapters.label: ch:spanish-subjuntivo-regular
chapters.canDo: I can form the singular present subjunctive of a regular verb in any of the three families.

payoff.summary: hable, coma, viva - the vowels swap sides, and -er and -ir agree again.

chapters.title: The Subjunctive Built From the Yo Form
chapters.label: ch:spanish-subjuntivo-yo-stem
chapters.canDo: I can build the subjunctive of an irregular verb from its yo form.

payoff.summary: quiera, pueda, haga - each one is its own yo form with the vowel swapped.

chapters.title: Ojala --- a Prayer That Outlived Its Religion
chapters.label: ch:spanish-ojala
chapters.canDo: I can wish for something with ojala, and say where the word came from.

payoff.summary: wa-sha' allah, carried through al-Andalus and kept long after.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Claiming, and Not Claiming
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-subjuntivo
chapters.canDo: I can choose the mood by deciding whether I am willing to assert the thing at all.

payoff.summary: Indicative: this is so. Subjunctive: I am not saying this is so.

chapters.title: Habla --- Telling Somebody To Do Something
chapters.label: ch:command-tu
chapters.canDo: I can give an informal positive command using a form I already hold.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-habla: give a tu command and name the form it reuses.
payoff.note: Costs nothing: the tu command IS the he/she present. Spanish reuses a form and lets context sort it out.

chapters.title: Di, Haz, Ve, Pon, Ten, Sal, Se, Ven
chapters.label: ch:command-irregular
chapters.canDo: I can use the eight irregular informal commands and say why they are all one syllable.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-ocho-cortos: give the eight forms and say why they are so short.
payoff.note: Not eight arbitrary exceptions: what the eight most-shouted verbs look like after two thousand years of being shouted.

chapters.title: No Hables --- Telling Somebody Not To
chapters.label: ch:command-negative
chapters.canDo: I can give a negative informal command, and say why it takes the subjunctive.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-no-hables: produce no hables and say why the subjunctive is the right form.
payoff.note: Not a borrowing: no hables asserts no speaking at all, so the non-asserting form is doing exactly its usual job.

chapters.title: Hable Usted --- The Polite Command
chapters.label: ch:command-usted
chapters.canDo: I can give a formal command and say why the usted form is the polite one.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-hable-usted: produce hable por favor and explain why the usted command is polite.
payoff.note: Usted is a worn-down title, so the order is aimed past the listener rather than at them -- and that indirectness IS the politeness.

chapters.title: Review --- Four Boxes
chapters.label: ch:review-commands
chapters.canDo: I can give all four command forms of a regular verb.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-repaso-mandatos: give all four boxes for comer and say what the rung genuinely cost.
payoff.note: A whole mood whose only new material was eight one-syllable words. The messiest box is the most-used one, as it has been for every irregularity in the book.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Asking Without Sounding Rude
chapters.label: ch:synthesis-commands
chapters.canDo: I can pick the command form that matches my relationship to the listener.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C50-sintesis-pedir-bien: command a friend and a stranger, and say where a Spanish command's politeness lives.
payoff.note: The English speaker's mistake here is not tone but person: politeness lives in the tu/usted choice, made before the command was spoken.

chapters.title: Lo Siento
chapters.label: ch:spanish-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Spanish and choose between lo siento and perdón.

payoff.summary: Say lo siento for regret and perdón for fault or for catching someone's attention, hearing sentir — I feel it — inside the first and dōnāre — to give completely — inside the second.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:spanish-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name all seven days of the week in Spanish and say why the last two broke away from the planet names.

payoff.summary: Run lunes to domingo straight through, then pair each weekend day against its English twin — sábado against Saturn's day, domingo against the Sun's.

chapters.title: Black, White, Red, and Blue
chapters.label: ch:spanish-black-white-red-blue
chapters.canDo: I can name black, white, red and blue in Spanish and say which of them Spanish borrowed rather than inherited.

payoff.summary: Say negro, blanco, rojo and azul, then sort them by origin: negro inherited from Latin, blanco traditionally linked to the Germanic Visigoths, rojo a cousin of English red by a different Latin branch, and azul carried in from Arabic lāzaward.

chapters.title: Parents and Siblings
chapters.label: ch:spanish-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my parents and my siblings in Spanish and explain why hermano is not built on Latin's word for brother.

payoff.summary: Give el padre, la madre, el hermano and la hermana, trace hermano back through germānus to germen, the seed, rather than to frāter, and separate its silent h from the once-spoken h of hijo and hacer.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:spanish-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Spanish and get la mano's gender right despite its -o ending.

payoff.summary: Say la cabeza and la mano, use me duele la mano, and explain the feminine article on a word that ends in -o by way of Latin's fourth declension.

chapters.title: The Seasons
chapters.label: ch:spanish-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name the four seasons in Spanish and explain how verano moved from spring to summer.

payoff.summary: Run primavera, verano, otoño, invierno, unpack primavera as prīma vēra, and show verano growing out of that same vēr before its meaning slid across to summer.

chapters.title: Water, Wine, and Bread
chapters.label: ch:spanish-water-wine-bread
chapters.canDo: I can name water, wine and bread in Spanish and say why a compañero is someone who shares bread with me.

payoff.summary: Say el agua, el vino and el pan, then open compañero into com- plus pānis and follow the root out to panadería and panadero.

chapters.title: La Bebo --- The Pronoun Tells the Truth
chapters.label: ch:pronoun-evidence
chapters.canDo: I can use an object pronoun to reveal a gender the article hides.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C55-la-bebo: say la bebo for el agua and explain why the pronoun can report a gender the article hides.
payoff.note: A third proof, after the adjective and the plural, and the cheapest of the three: nothing sits in front of a pronoun, so no vowels collide and it reports the gender straight. Turns a memorised exception into a test the reader can run.

chapters.title: The Months
chapters.label: ch:spanish-months
chapters.canDo: I can name the twelve months in Spanish and explain why diciembre carries the Latin word for ten.

payoff.summary: Recite enero through diciembre, tie marzo back to martes through Mars, and place septiembre and diciembre against the Roman year that started in March.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:spanish-noon-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say that it is noon or midnight in Spanish and break both words into their two living halves.

payoff.summary: Say es mediodía and es medianoche, split each into medio/media plus día/noche, and set them against French's worn-down midi and minuit.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:spanish-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can tell the time in Spanish and choose correctly between es la una and son las dos.

payoff.summary: Say es la una, son las dos, son las diez, and explain why one o'clock takes a singular verb while every other hour takes a plural one.

chapters.title: The Weather
chapters.label: ch:spanish-weather
chapters.canDo: I can talk about the weather in Spanish and know why llueve refuses to join hace.

payoff.summary: Ask about el tiempo, answer hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, then switch to llueve — a verb of its own, whose ll- is the same sound change that gave llamar.

chapters.title: Numbers Eleven to Twenty
chapters.label: ch:spanish-numbers-eleven-to-twenty
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Spanish and say where the fused Latin teens stop and the ten-and-X ones begin.

payoff.summary: Run once to quince as fused Latin compounds, then dieciséis to diecinueve as a ten-and-X template, say why Latin's own subtractive 18 and 19 did not survive, and close on veinte.

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:spanish-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Spanish and say which of the two words still has no agreed origin.

payoff.summary: Say gato and perro, trace cattus back toward Egypt, then admit that perro — which pushed out the older can — has no settled etymology at all.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:spanish-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can name green and yellow in Spanish and explain why amarillo is built on the word for bitter.

payoff.summary: Say verde and amarillo, tie verde to virēre, to flourish, and amarillo to amarellus, a little bitter — the same root as everyday amargo.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- Saying Something About Your Own Life
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-describing
chapters.canDo: I can describe things around me with the nouns and colours I hold, choosing un rather than el.

payoff.summary: Fourteen chapters of nouns and colours, combined for the first time - and the article that makes it possible.

chapters.title: Pensar — Thinking Is Weighing
chapters.label: ch:spanish-pensar
chapters.canDo: I can say what I think, and break pensar's stem the way a stem-changer requires.

payoff.summary: Run pensar through the e→ie boot, and find the scales still inside pensive and peso.

chapters.title: Entender — Understanding Is Stretching Toward
chapters.label: ch:spanish-entender
chapters.canDo: I can say what I understand, and see the verb inside the no entiendo I have used since chapter 14.

payoff.summary: The second e→ie stem-changer, and the moment a chapter-14 formula turns out to have parts.

chapters.title: Leer — Reading Is Gathering
chapters.label: ch:spanish-leer
chapters.canDo: I can say what I read, with a verb whose stem does not break.

payoff.summary: legere, the root that gathers: collect, select, elect, and intellect.

chapters.title: Escribir — Writing Is Scratching
chapters.label: ch:spanish-escribir
chapters.canDo: I can say what I write, and explain the propped-up e- in front of it.

payoff.summary: scrībere, to scratch, and Spanish refusing to begin a word with sc-.

chapters.title: Review --- Four Verbs of the Mind
chapters.label: ch:spanish-review-verbs-of-mind
chapters.canDo: I can hold all four mind-verbs at once and name the physical act inside each one.

payoff.summary: Four abstractions, four labourers: weighing, stretching, gathering, scratching.

chapters.title: Synthesis --- What You Understand, and What You Don't
chapters.label: ch:spanish-synthesis-verbs-of-mind

chapters.title: Hearing, Sleeping, Walking, Running
chapters.label: ch:spanish-hear-sleep-walk-run

payoff.summary: Run the chapter's four verbs together and sort them by what they do to their stems: correr, caminar and andar leave theirs alone, dormir breaks o to ue, oír grows a g in oigo and writes y in oyes. Then name each verb's source in turn — audīre, dormīre, Gaulish camminus, currere — and set the two words with no settled origin, andar and perro, against them.

chapters.title: Opening, Closing, Sitting Down, Standing Up

payoff.summary: Say the chapter in one breath — abro el libro, me siento, cierro el libro, me levanto — then separate the two features it taught: sentarse is reflexive and a stem-changer, levantarse is reflexive only. Name the shared recipe behind both body-position verbs (a Latin present participle, sedēns and levāns), pick abierto out as the one irregular participle, and reach back to la mano for why the article stays feminine.

chapters.title: Telling What Happened

payoff.summary: Tell a four-sentence story out loud: Llovía. Me levanté, luego bebí café. No corrí, porque llovía mucho. Me senté y leí. Every word in it has been taught in this book, and the two pasts divide the work between scene and event.

chapters.title: Waiting, Answering, Buying
chapters.label: ch:spanish-wait-answer-buy
chapters.canDo: I can say I wait, answer and buy in Spanish — three verbs whose endings never surprise me — and I know that esperar alone carries wait, hope and expect, so context does the work English hands to three separate verbs.

payoff.summary: Run espero, contesto and compro — three verbs that break nothing, whose whole difficulty is meaning — and give each root and its sense: spērāre to hope, contestārī to call witnesses, comparāre to procure. Refuse the lookalike: English compare descends from a different Latin comparāre built on compār, so it is not a relative. Then buy — compro el pan, el vino y un café, por favor — and reach back for what pānis gave compañero, which English words vīnum reached, why café is masculine, and what por favor says word for word.

chapters.title: Saying Why

payoff.summary: Answer ¿Por qué no corres? in four moves — Creo que llueve. No corro porque llueve, así que leo. Debo estudiar. Opinion, cause, consequence, obligation, each with its own word, and every word in it taught by this book.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C52-como-se-dice: ask the question politely and say why it is impersonal rather than aimed at the listener.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C52-tres-ses: say which two se's are one word and what marks the impostor.

payoff.note: The error that outlives the others, because the learner thinks the English first and the gap is invisible. English can delete the joint because its word order is rigid; Spanish moves its pieces, so it cannot.
